newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso sees re-election dream take life.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso sees re-election dream take life.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's hopes for an unprecedented second term were bolstered on Tuesday as Congress began considering proposals to allow for his re-election.
A 30-member committee convened to decide a constitutional amendment to permit presidents, state governors and mayors to run for a second, consecutive period in office.
"This is historic because no president has ever been able to stand for re-election," said Brasilia University politics professor David Fleischer.

Since the Brazilian Republic was founded in 1889, the constitution has forced holders of executive office to stand down after one term. Even the generals of the 1964-85 military dictatorship observed the tradition of alternating in power.
But Cardoso, halfway through a four-year term and struggling to push his reforms through Congress, wants to be a candidate in the 1998 presidential elections.

Analysts say six more Cardoso years would reassure investors that pro-market policies are firmly rooted. U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch, a critic of Brazilian policy, said recently that re-election for Cardoso represents the best chance of sustaining the new climate of low inflation after years of economic chaos.
The amendment is expected to pass through the committee, which is packed with deputies in favour of the reform and is being boycotted by opposition parties.

It will face a tougher time in the full Chamber of Deputies in January, where it will be voted on twice before being sent to the Senate. Polls have shown less than half of Brazil's deputies agree that Cardoso should have the chance of a second term.
"The president will probably get his way but it won't be until March or April and it will be at some cost," said Fleischer.

He said a cabinet reshuffle expected early next year and ongoing negotiations over the debts of state governments with Brasilia put the government in a strong position to negotiate for support in Congress.
